data.title: Hradište pod Vrátnom – hillforts guarding the Brezová Pass
data.excerpt: Hradište pod Vrátnom lies on the western foothills of the Lesser Carpathians, in the area of the original Principality of Moravia, in the valley of the Brezovský potok that had already served in prehistory as a route to the Brezová Pass. Two hillforts guarded the crossing — a large one of 1.5 ha above the quarry at u Fajnorov, in use from the 7th to the 12th century, and a smaller one on the hill known as Tomišovec. At the foot of Cigánka lay a row cemetery used in the 9th and early 10th century.
data.metaTitle: Hradište pod Vrátnom – hillforts at a Carpathian pass
data.metaDescription: Hradište pod Vrátnom lies on the western edge of the Lesser Carpathians, where two early medieval hillforts guarded the old route to the Brezová Pass.

children.text: Hradište pod Vrátnom lies on the western foothills of the Lesser Carpathians, that is, in the area of the original Principality of Moravia. So far I have managed to obtain only a minimum of information about it, but should I come across anything more detailed, it will certainly be added.

Hradište grew up in the valley of the Brezovský potok, which had already been used in prehistory as a route to the Brezová Pass, a convenient crossing of the Lesser Carpathians from the Záhorie region to the Váh region.

children.text: The presence of man in these parts as early as the Old Stone Age (the Palaeolithic) is attested by a find of charcoal embedded in travertine on the right-hand side of the highway from Hradište to Brezová. Polished stone tools of the New Stone Age (the Neolithic) have also been found at several places in the valley. Finds at Osuské, in the cadastral area of Hradište and at Štverník show that the pass was a scene of lively activity in the Bronze Age (1800–700 BC) as well. The pass gained great importance after the arrival of the Slavs at the beginning of the 6th century. They also built hillforts to protect it: a large one, with a fortified area of 1.5 ha, above the quarry in the hamlet of u Fajnorov beyond Košariská, though already within the cadastral area of the village of Prašník, which was in use from the 7th to the 12th century.

A relatively small hillfort also grew up in the cadastral area of Hradište, above the village on the hill known as “Tomišovec”, below whose steep slope the Brezovský potok flows. Judging by the sherds found there, it was built in the Middle Hillfort period, in the 9th–10th century. This hillfort on the right bank of the stream and, facing it on the opposite bank, the travertine rocks that once reached as far as the boggy meadows gripped the valley at this point like the jaws of a great pair of pincers! The road had to skirt it in an arc above the rocks, by way of Babiná.

Guard duty at the hillfort was performed by men from a nearby settlement, which was likewise sited very practically and deliberately in a side valley on the left bank, so as to control the crossing of the Lesser Carpathians towards Dobrá Voda. From 1263 the entrance to it was protected on the southern side by Dobrá Voda Castle. At the upper end of the settlement, on a terrace at the foot of the Cigánka hill, there was a small row cemetery (4 graves, mostly without grave goods) from the end of the Great Moravian and the beginning of the post-Great Moravian period. It was discovered at the end of the holdings of J. Kováč and of the brothers V. Š. and A. Furko. The finds were rescued by a local resident, Florián Vulgan, who handed them over to representatives of the then archaeological institute in Trenčiansky Svätý Martin.

The more significant finds come from the foot of the Cigánka hill. In 1935 A. Furko struck human bones in his own yard. The grave was examined by Viktor Šemmer, who found a small knife, a fire-steel and a flint strike-a-light beside the skeleton.
Only 10 cm above the skeleton he recorded a layer of earth mixed with charcoal and ash, about 4–5 cm thick.

An inhumation grave with a decorated clay vessel had already been found earlier at the same spot. In the autumn of 1935 Viktor Šemmer examined two more graves, in which he found two small knives and a whetstone.

A few years later at least 20 graves were destroyed during work in the neighbouring yards. In 1946 Vojtech Budinský-Krička carried out a rescue excavation and examined four more graves, one of which was fitted with a timber structure, which points to the higher social standing of the person buried. Several further graves were damaged in 1956 and 1972. Burials were made in this medium-sized cemetery in the 9th and at the beginning of the 10th century.

Occupation of the area continued after the demise of Great Moravia and during the formation of the Kingdom of Hungary. On the slope north of Hradište pod Vrátnom, at the locality known as Tomišovec, Vladimír Jamárik collected in 1971 a large number of decorated and undecorated sherds from the 10th–12th century.
